title: Lift Up Your Heads, O Gates: The King of Glory
summary: The psalm opens by declaring that the earth and everyone in it belong to the LORD, who founded the world on the seas. It asks who may climb the LORD's hill and stand in his holy place, and answers: those with clean hands and a pure heart. It closes with a processional call to the ancient gates to lift their heads so that the King of Glory, the LORD mighty in battle, the LORD of Hosts, may enter.
story: Psalm 24 closes the group that begins with Psalm 15, which asks almost the same question: who may dwell on God's holy hill. Framing the collection this way places the royal psalms, the laments, and the praise of God's law inside a question about worship: who can come near? Coming after the shepherd of Psalm 23, whose guest dwells in the house of the LORD forever, Psalm 24 shows the procession toward that house. Its picture of God entering his city as a victorious king connects with the story of the ark, the chest that symbolized God's throne, being carried up to Jerusalem, and it points forward to the Bible's hope that God will come to dwell with his people.
historical:
The heading reads A Psalm of David. The ancient Greek translation adds that it is for the first day of the week, and a Jewish tradition preserved in the Mishnah (tractate Tamid) lists Psalm 24 as the psalm the Levites sang in the temple on the first day of the week. Many readers, ancient and modern, connect the psalm with David bringing the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem with shouting and music (2 Samuel 6:12-15), though the psalm itself doesn't say so. Others see it as a liturgy for a regular festival procession to the temple, perhaps repeated over generations, in which the ark or the worshipers came up to the gates. Those who date the psalm later point to the temple setting; those who hold to Davidic authorship point to the ark's arrival in the city David captured.

The question of who may ascend may reflect an actual gate ritual. Pilgrims approaching the sanctuary asked what was required to enter, and priests or Levites answered with a summary of the covenant's demands, as in Psalm 15 and Isaiah 33:14-16.
cultural:
The first two verses answer a common ancient belief. Many peoples pictured the world as established after a god's victory over the chaotic sea, and the storm god's defeat of the sea appears in Canaanite texts from Ugarit. Psalm 24 says simply that the LORD founded the earth upon the seas; the waters are not a rival but a foundation he laid. Because he made it, it is his, and everyone who lives in it belongs to him.

City gates in the ancient world were massive structures, often with towers, and their lintels (the beams across the top) could be pictured as heads. The poetic call for the gates to lift their heads treats them as if they must stand taller to admit a king of such size and glory. The title LORD of Hosts refers to God as commander of armies, both Israel's and the armies of heaven, and it was closely connected with the ark, which Israel carried into battle (1 Samuel 4:4).
literary: The psalm has three parts, and many scholars read it as a processional liturgy with alternating voices. Verses 1 and 2 are a short hymn to the creator. Verses 3 to 6 are an entrance liturgy: a question (Who may ascend?), an answer describing the worshiper, and a promise of blessing. Verses 7 to 10 are an antiphonal exchange at the gates, in which one group calls for the gates to open and another, perhaps the gatekeepers, asks, Who is this King of Glory? The exchange happens twice, and the second answer is fuller: not only the LORD mighty in battle, but the LORD of Hosts. The word Selah closes both the second and the third parts. The movement is from the whole earth, to the hill and the worshiper, to the gates and the King himself.

outline.t: Who may ascend the hill of the LORD?
Lift up your heads: the LORD mighty in battle
Lift up your heads: the LORD of Hosts is the King of Glory

doctrines.note: Because God founded the world, the world and all who live in it belong to him. Ownership follows from making, and no nation, ruler, or person holds the earth except as God's tenant.
Approaching God requires clean hands and a pure heart, integrity in action and in motive, along with refusal of idols and false oaths. The psalm pairs outward conduct and inward loyalty.
The LORD enters his city as King of Glory, victorious in battle. The psalm confesses God's kingship over creation and his presence among his people.

words.note: Kavod, glory. The root has to do with weight or heaviness, and the word came to mean the weight of a person's importance, honor, or splendor. Used of God, it often refers to his visible, overwhelming presence, as when his glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34). It appears five times in the closing verses: the King of Glory.

Shav, emptiness, falsehood, vanity. In verse 4 lifting up the soul to shav probably means trusting in an idol, something empty. The same word appears in the third commandment against taking God's name in vain (Exodus 20:7). The psalm links worthless worship with false speech.

Tseva'ot, hosts or armies. The LORD of Hosts presents God as commander of the heavenly armies and of Israel's forces. The title is closely tied to the ark (1 Samuel 4:4) and is the climactic answer to who the King of Glory is.

Naqi, innocent, clean, free from guilt. Clean hands in verse 4 are hands innocent of violence and wrongdoing. The same word describes innocent blood. It speaks of conduct, while the pure heart speaks of motive.

christ: Paul quotes verse 1 in 1 Corinthians 10:26, “The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof”, to teach that believers may eat food sold in the market with a clear conscience, because everything belongs to God. The rest of the psalm has also shaped Christian reading of Christ. The question of who may ascend God's hill with clean hands and a pure heart finds only one full answer in the New Testament's view, the sinless Christ who ascended into heaven, and who by his sacrifice brings his people with him (Hebrews 9:24, 10:19-22). Jesus' words, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8), echo the psalm's language. Christian worship has long sung verses 7 to 10 at Christ's ascension and at the coming of Christ in Advent, hearing in the King of Glory the risen Lord entering heaven or entering his people's lives. These are readings of the psalm in light of Christ rather than predictions the psalm itself makes, but the New Testament does call Jesus the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8).
questions: If the earth and everyone in it belongs to God, how does that change the way you think about your possessions, your work, or the people around you?
The psalm asks for clean hands and a pure heart. Which is harder for you, integrity in what you do or integrity in why you do it?
The gates are told to lift their heads for the King of Glory. What would it mean for you to open some part of your life that has been shut to him?
